#Text=By the end of some October, when its leaves have fallen, I frequently
#Text= see such a central sprig, whose progress I have watched, when I
#Text= thought it had forgotten its destiny, as I had, bearing its first crop
#Text= of small green or yellow or rosy fruit, which the cows cannot get at
#Text= over the bushy and thorny hedge which surrounds it, and I make haste
#Text= to taste the new and undescribed variety.
#Text=We have all heard of the
#Text= numerous varieties of fruit invented by Van Mons and Knight.
#Text=This is
#Text= the system of Van Cow, and she has invented far more and more
#Text= memorable varieties than both of them.
#Text=Through what hardships it may attain to bear a sweet fruit!
#Text=Though
#Text= somewhat small, it may prove equal, if not superior, in flavor to that
#Text= which has grown in a garden,--will perchance be all the sweeter and
#Text= more palatable for the very difficulties it has had to contend with.
#Text=Who knows but this chance wild fruit, planted by a cow or a bird on
#Text= some remote and rocky hillside, where it is as yet unobserved by man.
#Text=THE FRUIT, AND ITS FLAVOR
#Text=
#Text= The time for wild apples is the last of October and the first of
#Text= November.
#Text=They then get to be palatable, for they ripen late, and they
#Text= are still perhaps as beautiful as ever.
#Text=I make a great account of
#Text= these fruits, which the farmers do not think it worth the while to
#Text= gather,--wild flavors of the Muse, vivacious and inspiriting.
#Text=The
#Text= farmer thinks that he has better in his barrels, but he is mistaken,
#Text= unless he has a walker  '  s appetite and imagination, neither of which
#Text= can he have.
#Text=Such as grow quite wild, and are left out till the first of November,
#Text= I presume that the owner does not mean to gather.
#Text=They belong to
#Text= children as wild as themselves,--to certain active boys that I
#Text= know,--to the wild-eyed woman of the fields, to whom nothing comes
#Text= amiss, who gleans after all the world, and, moreover, to us walkers.
#Text=We have met with them, and they are ours.
#Text=These rights, long enough
#Text= insisted upon, have come to be an institution in some old countries,
#Text= where they have learned how to live.
#Text=I hear that "the custom of
#Text= grippling, which may be called apple-gleaning, is, or was formerly,
#Text=America," though they are more memorable to my taste than the grafted
#Text= kinds; more racy and wild American flavors do they possess when
#Text= October and November, when December and January, and perhaps February
#Text= and March even, have assuaged them somewhat.
#Text=An old farmer in my
#Text= neighborhood, who always selects the right word, says that "they have
#Text= a kind of bow-arrow tang."
#Text=Apples for grafting appear to have been selected commonly, not so much
#Text= for their spirited flavor, as for their mildness, their size, and
#Text= bearing qualities,--not so much for their beauty, as for their
#Text= fairness and soundness.
#Text=Indeed, I have no faith in the selected lists
#Text= of pomological gentlemen.
#Text=Their "Favorites" and "None-suches" and
#Text= "Seek-no-farthers," when I have fruited them, commonly turn out very
#Text= tame and forgettable.
#Text=They are eaten with comparatively little zest,
#Text= and have no real _tang_ nor _smack_ to them.
#Text=What if some of these wildings are acrid and puckery, genuine
#Text= _verjuice_, do they not still belong to the _Pomaceæ_, which are
#Text= uniformly innocent and kind to our race?
#Text=I still begrudge them to the
#Text= cider-mill.
#Text=Perhaps they are not fairly ripe yet.
#Text=No wonder that these small and high-colored apples are thought to make
#Text= the best cider.
#Text=Loudon quotes from the "Herefordshire Report," that
#Text= "apples of a small size are always, if equal in quality, to be
#Text= preferred to those of a larger size, in order that the rind and kernel
#Text= may bear the greatest proportion to the pulp, which affords the
#Text= weakest and most watery juice."

#Text=Of course no flavors are thrown away; they are intended for the taste
#Text= that is up to them.
#Text=Some apples have two distinct flavors, and perhaps
#Text= one half of them must be eaten in the house, the other outdoors.
#Text=One
#Text= Peter Whitney wrote from Northborough in 1782, for the Proceedings of
#Text= the Boston Academy, describing an apple tree in that town "producing
#Text= fruit of opposite qualities, part of the same apple being frequently
#Text=sour and the other sweet;" also some all sour, and others all sweet,
#Text= and this diversity on all parts of the tree.
#Text=There is a wild apple on Nawshawtuct Hill in my town which has to me a
#Text= peculiarly pleasant bitter tang, not perceived till it is
#Text= three-quarters tasted.
#Text=It remains on the tongue.
#Text=As you eat it, it
#Text= smells exactly like a squash-bug.
#Text=It is a sort of triumph to eat and
#Text= relish it.
#Text=I hear that the fruit of a kind of plum tree in Provence is "called
#Text= _Prunes sibarelles_, because it is impossible to whistle after having
#Text= eaten them, from their sourness."
#Text=But perhaps they were only eaten in
#Text= the house and in summer, and if tried out-of-doors in a stinging
#Text= atmosphere, who knows but you could whistle an octave higher and
#Text= clearer?
#Text=In the fields only are the sours and bitters of Nature appreciated;
#Text= just as the woodchopper eats his meal in a sunny glade, in the middle
#Text= of a winter day, with content, basks in a sunny ray there, and dreams
#Text= of summer in a degree of cold which, experienced in a chamber, would
#Text=make a student miserable.
#Text=They who are at work abroad are not cold,
#Text= but rather it is they who sit shivering in houses.
#Text=As with
#Text= temperatures, so with flavors; as with cold and heat, so with sour and
#Text= sweet.
#Text=This natural raciness, the sours and bitters which the diseased
#Text= palate refuses, are the true condiments.
#Text=Let your condiments be in the condition of your senses.
#Text=To appreciate
#Text= the flavor of these wild apples requires vigorous and healthy senses,
#Text= _papillæ_ firm and erect on the tongue and palate, not easily
#Text= flattened and tamed.
#Text=From my experience with wild apples, I can understand that there may
#Text= be reason for a savage  '  s preferring many kinds of food which the
#Text= civilized man rejects.
#Text=The former has the palate of an outdoor man.
#Text=It
#Text= takes a savage or wild taste to appreciate a wild fruit.
#Text=What a healthy out-of-door appetite it takes to relish the apple of
#Text= life, the apple of the world, then!
